speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy is strong overall and has made significant progress toward our goals over the past two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market has cooled from its formerly overheated state and remains solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased substantially from a peak of 7 percent to 2.1 percent as of September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are committed to maintaining our economy’s strength by supporting maximum employment and returning inflation to our 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today, the FOMC decided to take another step in reducing the degree of policy restraint by lowering our policy interest rate by ¼ percentage point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We continue to be confident that, with an appropriate recalibration of our policy stance, strength in the economy and the labor market can be maintained, with inflation moving sustainably down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also decided to continue to reduce our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that economic activity has continued to expand at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: GDP rose at an annual rate of 2.8 percent in the third quarter, about the same pace as in the second quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Growth of consumer spending has remained resilient, and investment in equipment and intangibles has strengthened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In contrast, activity in the housing sector has been weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, improving supply conditions have supported the strong performance of the U.S. economy over the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, conditions remain solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll job gains have slowed from earlier in the year, averaging 104,000 per month over the past three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This figure would have been somewhat higher were it not for the effects of labor strikes and hurricanes on employment in October.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Regarding the hurricanes, let me extend our sympathies to all the families, businesses, and communities who have been harm—harmed by these devastating storms.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate is notably higher than it was a year ago but has edged down over the past three months and remains low at 4.1 percent in October.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nominal wage growth has eased over the past year, and the jobs-to-workers gap has narrowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, a broad set of indicators suggests that conditions in the labor market are now less tight than just before the pandemic in 2019.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market is not a source of significant inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased significantly over the past two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Total PCE prices rose 2.1 percent over the 12 months ending in September; excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.7 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, inflation has moved much closer to our 2 percent longer-run goal, but core inflation remains somewhat elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Longer-term inflation expectations appear to remain well anchored, as reflected in a broad range of surveys of households, businesses, and forecasters, as well as measures from financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see the risks to achieving our employment and inflation goals as being roughly in balance, and we’re attentive to the risks to both sides of our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by ¼ percentage point, to 4½ percent to 4¾ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This further recalibration of our policy stance will help maintain the strength of the economy and the labor market and will continue to enable further progress on inflation as we move toward a more neutral stance over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that reducing policy strain—restraint too quickly could hinder progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, reducing policy restraint too slowly could unduly weaken economic activity and employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In considering additional adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will carefully assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are not on any preset course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to make our decisions meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As the economy evolves, monetary policy will adjust in order to best promote our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the economy remains strong and inflation is not sustainably moving toward 2 percent, we can dial back policy restraint more slowly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the labor market were to weaken unexpectedly or inflation were to fall more quickly than anticipated, we can move more quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Policy is well positioned to deal with the risks and uncertainties that we face in pursuing both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy—maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation sustainably to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our affect—actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I look forward to our discussion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So let me say that in the near term, the election will have no effects on our policy decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As you know, many, many things affect the economy, and anyone who writes down forecasts in their job will tell you that the economy is quite difficult to forecast, looking out past the very near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Here, we don’t know what the timing and substance of any policy changes will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We therefore don’t know what the effects on the economy would be—specifically, whether and to what extent those policies would matter for the achievement of our goal variables: maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t—we don’t guess, we don’t speculate, and we don’t assume.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, just in principle, it’s possible that any Administration’s policies or, or policies put in place by Congress could have economic effects over time—over time that would matter for our pursuit of our dual-mandate goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, we—along with countless other factors, forecasts of those economic effects would be included in our models of the economy and would be taken into account through that channel.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would just say this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve watched the, the run-up in bond rates, and it’s, it’s nowhere where it was, of course, a year ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I guess that, you know, the long- run rates are well below that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re watching that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Things have been moving around, and we’ll see where they settle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it’s too early to really say where they settle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Ultimately, I’m sure we’ve all read these decompositions of what, you know—and I certainly have, but it’s not really our job to provide our specific decomposition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will say, though, that it appears that the moves are not, not principally about higher inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re really about a sense of more likely to have stronger growth and perhaps less in the way of downside risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what they’re about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we do take financial conditions into account.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If they—if they’re persistent and if they’re material, then we’ll certainly take them into account in our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I would say we’re not at—we’re not at that stage right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just something that we’re watching.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, again, these things don’t really have mainly to do with, with Fed policy, but to do with other factors in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—you get halfway through the cycle between the last set and the next set.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I wouldn’t want to comment one way or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, people are—let’s talk about the data we’ve gotten since the last meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, in the main, the economic activity data have been stronger than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The NIPA revision was stronger.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Certainly, the September employment report was stronger; the October report, not stronger; retail sales, stronger.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, overall, though, I think you take away a sense of, of some of the downside risks to economic activity having, having been diminished, with the NIPA revisions in particular, and so, overall, feeling, feeling good about economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think we would factor that in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, we got one inflation report, which was—it wasn’t terrible, but it was—it was a little higher than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think, really, the question is, is December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, by December we’ll have—we’ll have more data: I guess one more employment report, two more inflation reports, and lots of other data, and, you know, we’ll make a decision as we get to December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I can’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t fill out a—we don’t fill out an SEP, and I can’t characterize one that wasn’t filled out today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I can’t really speak for kind of exactly where the—where the Committee is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would just say, for December, we’re going to be—again, in every meeting—we’re going to be looking at the incoming data and how that affects the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As you know, we’re in the process of recalibrating from a fairly restrictive level at 5.33 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: After today’s move, we’re down 75 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re trying to, to be on a middle path where we can maintain the strength in the labor market while also enabling further progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think that’s where we are, but that’s the question we’re going to be asking in September and, and in other meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, again, I can’t really update you on the Committee’s thinking, because we don’t fill out an SEP at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, I’m going to wait—we’re going to wait and see how things come in in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I—it’s just—I would put it this way: We’re on a path to a more neutral stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and that’s very much what we’re on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That has not changed at all since September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we’re just going to have to see where the—where the data lead us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have, you know, a whole six weeks of data to look at to make that decision in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Obviously, I’m not ruling it out or in, but, but, you know, I would say—you know, I would say that, you know, again, we didn’t update the SEP, so I’m not going to characterize, you know, where the Committee would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Not really, no.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So let me tell you what we were thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we, we met that test in September, and therefore we take that test out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you leave it in, then it’s new forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s brand new forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The point is we have gained confidence that, that we’re on a sustainable path down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that, I would tell you, is, is what that’s really all about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s not meant to send a signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Neither of those is meant to send a further signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, saying “further progress” it becomes a test where we don’t want to be—we don’t think it’s a good time to be doing a lot of, of forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re—there’s a fair amount of uncertainty in that—in what I’ve said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The path that we’re on, we do know what—where the destination is, but we don’t know the right pace, and we don’t know exactly where the destination is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the—the—the point is to find that, to find the right pace and the right destination as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think there’s a fair amount of uncertainty about that, and, you know, you don’t want to tie yourself up with, with guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You want to be able to make sensible decisions as you go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we don’t comment on fiscal policy, and, again, I don’t have a lot more to say on, on what’s driving bond yields.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of, of policy changes, though, let me give you a sense of how this, this works in the ordinary case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Let’s say Congress is considering a rewrite of the tax laws; it doesn’t matter what’s in the content.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we would follow that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At a certain point, we’d, we’d think we see the outline, so we’d start to model it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then we’d wait, and we’d wait, and, at a certain point, the staff would brief the FOMC and say, you know, “This is—these are the likely effects.” There’s lots and lots of literature on the effects of tax policy changes on various parts of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’d, we’d try to get smart on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then the law actually passes, and, you know, you’d start to put it—you’d probably run an alternative simulation before that happens, just to keep people trying to understand it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Then, then when it actually passes, it goes into the model, along with a million other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, these—we have a very large economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Many things are affecting it at any given time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, a law change of some kind would go in there, but—it would go in, but it would—you know, it’s a process that takes some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Clearly, the legislative process takes a lot of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, the real question is not the effect of that law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s all of the policy changes that are happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think that’s a—that’s a process that takes a lot of time and that we go through all the time with every Administration, constantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I just—this will be no different.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, right now, we’re—there’s nothing to—there’s nothing to model right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s such an early stage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know what the policies are, and once we know what they are, we won’t—we won’t have a sense of, you know, when they’ll be implemented or, or all those sorts of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think I would just say— STEVE LIESMAN.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Mm-hmm.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: —we’re not doing that now, and all that will take time, and it will be very much regular order when we do do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you remember the 5 percent 10-year, people were drawing massively important conclusions only to find, you know, three weeks later that the 10-year was 50 basis points lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, it’s material changes and financial conditions that last, that are persistent, that really matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we don’t know that about these.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re watching it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re doing the decompositions and reading others, but right now it’s not a major factor in, in how we’re thinking about things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, and as you mentioned, the latest economic data have been strong, and that’s, of course, a great thing and highly welcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, of course, our mandate is maximum for employment and price stability, and we think that even with today’s cut, policy is still restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand it’s not possible to say precisely how restrictive, but we feel that it is still restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if you look at our goal variables, the labor market has cooled a great deal from its overheated state of two years ago and is now essentially in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is continuing to cool, albeit at a—at a modest rate, and we don’t need further cooling, we don’t think, to achieve our inflation mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has moved down a great deal from its higher—its highs of two years ago, and we judged, as I mentioned, that it’s on a sustainable path back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the job’s not done on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if you look at those two things, we judged in September that it was appropriate to begin to recalibrate our policy stance to reflect this progress, and today’s decision is really another step in that process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, as I mentioned, we believe that with an appropriate recalibration of our policy stance, we can maintain strength in the labor market even as our policy stance enables further progress toward our inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we haven’t, you know, made any decision like that at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’re—so we’re in the process, as I mentioned, of moving policy down—our stance down over time to a more neutral level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, as a general matter, as we move ahead, we are prepared to adjust our assessments of the appropriate pace and destination as the outlook evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, for example, if we were to see the labor market deteriorating, we’d be prepared to move more quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Alternatively, as we approach levels that are plausibly neutral or close to neutral, it may turn out to be appropriate to slow the pace at which we’re dialing back restriction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, haven’t made any decisions about that, but that’s certainly a possibility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you—you can think of it as similar to what we do with asset purchase—with asset runoff with QT.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we reach a point where we slow the pace, much like an airplane reaching the airport slows down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so, you know, it—we’re thinking about it that way, but it’s, it’s something that we’re just beginning to think about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, so I think if you look at the 3- and 6-month—you’re quoting the 12-month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if you look at three- and six-month core PCE, you’ll see they’re around 2.3 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we look at all of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we look at—we also—we look at 12 as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what it’s telling us is that we really have made significant progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we expect there to be bumps.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For example, you know, the, the last three months of last year, the core PCE readings were very, very low—probably unsustainably low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s why you see—that’s why forecasts generally see a couple of upticks toward the end of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: On the other hand, the January reading certainly looks like an example of residual seasonality, so that we saw last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So when that falls out of the 12-month calculation in February, we should see it staying down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there will literally be a bump up and then down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: One is the nonhousing services and goods, which together make up 80 percent of that—of the core PCE index, are back to the levels they were at the last time we had sustained 2 percent inflation, which happens to be in the early 2000s for a period of five, six, seven years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So they’re back at that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What’s not is housing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So let’s talk about housing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Housing services is higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What’s going on there is, you know, market rents, newly signed leases, are experiencing very low inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what’s happening is older, you know, leases that are turning over are taking several years to catch up to where market, market leases are—market rent leases are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s just a catch-up problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not really reflecting current inflationary pressures; it’s reflecting past inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s, that’s one thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The other thing is, I’d say look at the labor market—not a source of inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not a very tight economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You see that catch-up inflation also in insurance and in several other areas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re seeing—we’re not, not declaring victory, obviously, but we feel like the story is very consistent with inflation continuing to come down on a bumpy path over the next couple of years and settling around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That story is intact, and it won’t be one or two really good data months, or bad data months aren’t going to really change the pattern at this point, now that we’re this far into the process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nothing in the economic data suggests that the Committee has any need to be in a hurry to get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are seeing strong economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are seeing ongoing strength in the labor market; we’re watching that carefully, but we do see maintaining strength there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we think that the right way—the right way to find neutral, if you will, is carefully, patiently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, that’s not meant to have a specific meaning other than we—to the extent—to the extent the economy remains strong, we have the ability to, to take advantage of that as we try to navigate that middle path between the two risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So on your first question, I’m not going to talk about anything that relates directly or indirectly to the election.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: On the second one, you’re—you know, this is the great question, and it’s the one we think about all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’ll just say a couple things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, there’s nothing really surprising here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What we know is that the unemployment rate is low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also know that it’s come down significantly—sorry, moved up significantly from a year or so ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ve seen a big change upward in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sometimes that has meant bad things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So far, it doesn’t appear to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It appears that the—I wouldn’t say that the labor market has fully stabilized, because I do think it’s continuing to very gradually cool, but it seems to be in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And our policy, of course, is designed to keep it in that good place, to maintain the strength in the labor market, while also enabling further progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, you mentioned a bunch of, of indicators, and you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the, the openings to unemployment rate is back to a normal level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would—I would characterize it more broadly as “normalizing.” You mentioned wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wages are still running just a bit above where they would need to be to be consistent with 2 percent inflation, unless productivity is going to remain at this high level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we see the—if we see productivity, you know, more sustainably at these high levels, then that would sustain higher wage gains.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would say—in fact, you can say it the other way, that, that wage increases are now consistent with 2 percent inflation given current productivity readings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, of course, you know, the lore on productivity readings is whenever you see high readings, you should assume they’re going to revert pretty quickly to the longer-term trend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That has always been the case for 50 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, it may be that—we’re now five years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at the NIPA revisions that came out a month ago, we’re five years into, into a nice set of productivity readings, which are sustained and very healthy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, overall, it’s a good labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We could talk about 20 different data series.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll be looking at all of them, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, we don’t want the labor market to, to soften much from here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s hard to characterize a, you know, really interesting set of discussions we had, and, of course, you’ll see them in the minutes in three weeks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I would say this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think, you know, the comments from our Reserve Bank colleagues and from the CEOs that they talk to are pretty constructive on the economy right now—pretty constructive, feeling that the labor market is, is, you know, back to normal to the point where it’s no longer that much of a discussion topic in their world, whereas two years ago, it was all they were talking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So they feel like the labor market’s in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People feel good about where the economy is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Demand is obviously pretty strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, you’re seeing, what, 2.8 percent growth in the third quarter estimated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Maybe the year is 2½.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is—this is—you know, this is a strong economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s actually remarkable how well the U.S. economy has been performing with, you know, strong growth, a strong labor market, inflation coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re, you know, really performing better than any of our global peers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think that is reflected in what you hear from—what I hear people hear from CEOs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t get to talk to a lot of CEOs in my job, but I hear what others summarize from those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, I hear the Reserve Bank presidents do a lot of that, and it’s pretty constructive overall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, that’s not to say—there are areas of caution and things like that but, ultimately, overall pretty positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it’s—you know, it’s things like—clearly, geopolitical risks around the world are elevated, and just as clearly, they’ve had relatively little effect on the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, that can change through the price of oil or otherwise, but people talk about those as, you know, something that’s on the horizon all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, ultimately, if you look at the U.S. economy, its, its performance has been very good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s, that’s what we hear from businesspeople, an expectation that that will continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If anything, people feel next year—I’ve heard this from several people—that next year could even be stronger than this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, I have said many times no more, no less than what the predecessors you mentioned have said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what that is is that the U.S. fiscal—federal government’s fiscal path—fiscal policy is on an unsustainable path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The level of our debt relative to the economy is not unsustainable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The path is unsustainable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, you’ve got a very large deficit at—you’re at full employment, and that’s expected to continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s important that we—you know, that that be dealt with.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is ultimately a threat to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t have oversight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I was not referring to, to the new Administration’s policies at all, nor will I today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I—what I’m just saying is, as we look ahead, we know—and I mentioned this in my statement—that the risks are two sided.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I guess I should start by saying that we think that the economy and we think our policy are both in a very good place, a very good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have to avoid that risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that, that—to avoid that risk, that means you want to move carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The other risk is that we move too slowly and that we allow the labor market to weaken too much and do unnecessary damage to the labor market and to people’s working lives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That, that says, “Don’t get behind the curve.” So these are two—these two things are the two risks that we have to manage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we’re, we’re in the middle there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We try to be in the middle and deal with both of the—manage both of those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, the idea is to maintain support, the strength that we have in the labor market and in the economy, but also with somewhat less restrictive but still restrictive policy, enable further progress toward our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so there’s—you know, there—this is the thing: Meeting by meeting, we’re going to be making our assessment of what the right path is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s not as important—the precise timing of these things is not as important as the overall arc of them, and the arc of them is to move from where we are now to a sense of neutral, a more neutral policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know exactly where that is; we only know it by its works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re pretty sure it’s below where we are now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But as we move further, there will be more uncertainty about where that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re going to move carefully as, as this goes on so that, you know, we can increase the chances that we will get it right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we, we would be concerned if we saw—if we thought we saw longer-term inflation expectations anchoring at a higher level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s not what we’re seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re still seeing between surveys and market readings broadly consistent with—you know, I, I looked at the five-year, five-year earlier today, and it’s probably moved, but it’s just not—it’s just—it’s kind of right where it’s been, and also it’s pretty close to consistent with 2 percent PCE inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s one that’s been a traditional one that we look at a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, overall, expectations seem to be—and really have throughout this—in a place that’s consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you’re right to say we watch that very carefully, and we will not allow inflation expectations to drift upward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s, that’s really why we reacted so sharply back in 2022 was, was to avoid that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re right that, you know, we say that the economy is performing well, and it is, but we also know that people are still feeling the effects of high prices, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we went through—the world went through a global inflation shock, and inflation went up everywhere.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, it, it stays with you because the price level doesn’t come back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what that takes is it takes some years of real wage gains for people to feel better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what we’re—that’s what we’re trying to create.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think we’re well on the road to creating that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has come way down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy is still strong here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wages are moving up but, but at a sustainable level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s just—I think—I think what needs to happen is happening and, for the most part, has happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’ll be some time before people, you know, regain their confidence and feel that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we don’t tell people how to—how to feel about the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We respect—completely respect—what they’re feeling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those feelings are true; they’re accurate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t question them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We—you know, we respect them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not going—I’m not going to get into the—any of the political things here today, but thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s a—you know, the whole plan is not to have stagflation, so we don’t have to deal with it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s our—that is actually our plan.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: [Laughter] You know, it’s, of course, a very difficult thing because you’re—you know, you’re—anything you do with interest rates will, will hurt one side or the other, either the inflation mandate or the—or the employment mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would just say that, you know, we’ve, we’ve been able to see inflation come down a whole lot, you know, much closer to our goal without the kind of sharp increase in unemployment that has often accompanied programs of disinflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So knock on wood, we’ve gotten this far without seeing a real weakening in, in the labor market.

sentence: And we believe we can complete the inflation task while also keeping the labor market strong, and that, of course, is exactly what we’re trying to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t rule anything out or in that far away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s certainly not, not our plan.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, our baseline expectation is that we’ll continue to move gradually down towards neutral, that the economy will continue to grow at a healthy clip, and that the labor market will remain strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at our—look at our—that will not change from the September SEP. You know, that is our baseline forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, short of some exogenous event, it will—that will continue to be our forecast for the foreseeable future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

sentence: That’s, that’s not the way our framework works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re aiming for inflation at, at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re—we do not have—we do not think it would be appropriate to deliberately undershoot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, part of the problem there is that low inflation can be a problem, too, in a way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s not part of our framework, and it’s not something we’re going to be—going to be looking at in our framework review.

sentence: Thank you very much.
